teaching.causalExplanation: The same. Water adds volume, but it doesn't bring any sodium carbonate, and none can escape. Every particle that left the pipette is still in the flask. They're just spread through ten times the volume, so each millilitre holds a tenth as many. It's like topping up cordial with water. The drink tastes weaker, but the syrup you poured is all still in the glass. That's what dilution is: adding solvent to lower the concentration, while the amount of solute stays the same. To describe any dilution, chemists name three things. The stock is the solution you take from, here our standard, and its concentration is c one. The aliquot is the measured portion you transfer, and its volume is V one, twenty-five point zero zero millilitres. The final volume, V two, is the total after making up to the mark, two hundred and fifty point zero millilitres. Not the water you added. The total. Now follow the moles. In the aliquot, n equals c one times V one, with the volume in litres. Zero point one zero zero three times zero point zero two five zero zero is two point five zero eight times ten to the minus three moles. Those same moles end up in the flask. So the new concentration is that amount divided by zero point two five zero zero litres, which is zero point zero one zero zero three moles per litre. Ten times the volume, a tenth of the concentration.
